content: The use of floodgates on dams to manipulate larval habitats in areas with indoor residual spraying (IRS) has uncertain effects on clinical malaria incidence due to a high risk of bias and very serious imprecision. Observational data from one study with 271 participants in the intervention group and 299 in the comparator group showed no clear evidence of benefit. The evidence is of very low certainty. Malaria parasite prevalence across all ages was assessed in one observational study. At baseline, there were 271 participants in the intervention group and 299 in the comparator group. The data at follow-up were not provided. The evidence regarding the effect of flushing through floodgates on malaria parasite prevalence in areas with IRS is very uncertain due to serious risk of bias and very serious imprecision. Fifteen studies were included in a systematic review evaluating the use of larvivorous fish for malaria prevention. These studies were conducted in various countries, including Comoros, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Kenya, South Korea, Sri Lanka, Sudan, and Tajikistan. Treated aquatic habitats included wells, domestic water containers, fishponds, riverbed pools, rice fields, and canals. No studies reported on clinical malaria, entomological inoculation rates (EIR), or adult vector densities. Twelve studies reported on the density of immature vector stages, and five studies reported on the number of aquatic habitats positive for immature vector stages. The studies were not suitable for pooled analysis. The evidence is very uncertain about whether larvivorous fish reduce the density of immature vector stages compared to no fish. However, larvivorous fish may reduce the number of larval sites positive for immature vector stages, but the evidence is of very low certainty. Topical repellents were evaluated in eight studies, six of which were included in a meta-analysis. These studies were conducted in South America, Southeast Asia, and Africa. The evidence suggests that topical repellents may have little to no protective effect against Plasmodium falciparum infection or clinical malaria incidence. The certainty of the evidence is low due to serious risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. Insecticide-treated clothing was assessed in two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) conducted in Colombia (military personnel) and Pakistan (Afghan refugees). The evidence suggests that insecticide-treated clothing may reduce clinical malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, but the certainty of the evidence is low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. Spatial or airborne repellents were evaluated in two RCTs conducted in China and Indonesia. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of spatial repellents on malaria parasitemia compared to no spatial repellents. The certainty of the evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias, inconsistency, and imprecision. Space spraying was assessed in a single interrupted time series study from India, which reported monthly malaria incidence over a four-year period. The evidence is very uncertain about the effect of space spraying on monthly malaria cases compared to no space spraying. The certainty of the evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision. House screening (e.g., windows, ceilings, doors, and eaves) was evaluated in two cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs). One trial in Ethiopia assessed window and door screening, while another trial in Gambia assessed full screening (eaves, doors, windows, and ceilings). The evidence suggests that house screening may reduce the entomological inoculation rate (EIR) and clinical malaria incidence caused by Plasmodium falciparum. However, the certainty of the evidence is low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. House screening may have little to no effect on malaria parasite prevalence but probably reduces anemia prevalence. The certainty of the evidence for anemia reduction is moderate. Therapeutic courses of sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) were evaluated in observational studies. The evidence suggests that SP may improve low birth weight outcomes in low-burden areas and result in a large improvement in high-burden areas. SP may also decrease maternal anemia and probably reduces maternal malaria infection at delivery. The certainty of the evidence ranges from low to moderate, with upgrades due to a clear dose-response gradient but downgrades due to serious publication bias.
